## Introduction

### Context & overview

The Unix shell is great for many tasks other than the file browser-like ones
you learned about in the previous lecture.
One of those is performing basic viewing, querying, and editing operations on
text files.

Recall from the [Project File Organization lecture](../week02/w2a_project-org.qmd#use-plain-text-files)
that we'll almost exclusively use "**plain-text**" files in this course.
For example:

- Sequence and annotation file formats such as FASTA, FASTQ, and GTF
- Spreadsheet-like/tabular files stored as TSV/CSV
- Scripts and code notebooks
- Documentation files such as Markdown

The commands we'll discuss here can be used with plain-text files but not with
"binary" formats like Excel or Word files.
(The one exception is _compressed_ plain-text files, like our `.fastq.gz` files:
as you'll see, some tools can read those directly.)

### Learning goals

In this lecture, you will learn to use the Unix shell to:

- View the contents of text files in various ways
- Use redirection and the pipe to flexibly process the output of commands
- Search within, manipulate, and extract information from text files

## Viewing the contents of text files

Several commands can view all or part of one or more text files,
and we'll discuss the most common ones below.

### `cat`

The **`cat`** command prints the entire contents of one or more files to
screen:

```bash
cat metadata.tsv
```
```bash-out
sample_id       time    treatment
S82     10dpi   cathemerium
S75     10dpi   cathemerium
S79     10dpi   cathemerium
S83     10dpi   cathemerium
S78     10dpi   control
S84     10dpi   control
S77     10dpi   control
S81     10dpi   control
S76     10dpi   relictum
S80     10dpi   relictum
S85     10dpi   relictum
S86     10dpi   relictum
S64     24hpi   cathemerium
S67     24hpi   cathemerium
S70     24hpi   cathemerium
S66     24hpi   control
S69     24hpi   control
S63     24hpi   control
S71     24hpi   relictum
S74     24hpi   relictum
S65     24hpi   relictum
S68     24hpi   relictum
```

For reference, let's also open this file in the editor. Either:

- Find it in the **file explorer** in the sidebar and click on it, or
- **Hover** over the file name in the terminal and press <kbd>Cmd</kbd> (Mac) or
  <kbd>Ctrl</kbd> (Windows/Linux), and you should see it become underlined and
  clickable. Click it to open the file in the editor.

Especially when working with omics data, files can be huge,
and this is one reason we use commands instead of a text editor to work with them.
But `cat` is not always the best tool for viewing large files either:
printing a whole large file can take a while, and makes it hard to see the
beginning of the output. We'll explore some other options below.

### `head` and `tail`

The twin commands **`head`** and **`tail`** print only the
first (`head`) or last (`tail`) lines of a file.
By default, they print 10 lines:

```bash
head metadata.tsv
```
```bash-out
sample_id       time    treatment
S82     10dpi   cathemerium
S75     10dpi   cathemerium
S79     10dpi   cathemerium
S83     10dpi   cathemerium
S78     10dpi   control
S84     10dpi   control
S77     10dpi   control
S81     10dpi   control
S76     10dpi   relictum
```

Use the `-n` option to specify the number of lines to print:

```bash
head -n 3 metadata.tsv
```
```bash-out
sample_id       time    treatment
S82     10dpi   cathemerium
S75     10dpi   cathemerium
```

::: callout-note
#### Options that take an argument ([🤯]{style="font-size: 1.4em;"})

This is the first option we've seen that needs a value:
unlike the ON/OFF flags you saw so far, it has to be followed by a number.

- In `-n 3`, `3` is an argument of the option `-n`
  (cf. `metadata.tsv` is an argument of the command `head`).
- You don't need a space between the option and its argument:
  `head -n3 metadata.tsv` works the same as `head -n 3 metadata.tsv`.
:::

Let's try to take a peek inside a FASTQ file.
To print the first eight lines (two reads), use `-n 8` with `head`:

``` bash
head -n 8 S63_R1.fastq.gz
```

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>Ouch! 😳 What went wrong here? *(Click to see the answer)*</summary>
We were presented with the contents of the *compressed* file, which isn't human-readable.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Still: prefer to keep FASTQ files compressed! _(Click to expand)_

To get around the problem you just encountered with `head`,
you might be inclined to decompress these files
(e.g. with the `gunzip` command, which you'll use in next week's assignment).
However, at least when it comes to FASTQ files,
it is better to keep them compressed:

- Uncompressed files take up much more disk storage space than compressed ones.
- Almost any bioinformatics program accepts compressed FASTQ files.
- You _can_ view these files in compressed form, as shown below with `less`.
  Additionally, several commands including `cat` have a counterpart for compressed
  files (`zcat` in the case of `cat`).

Other genomics files, like assembly FASTA files and annotation GTF/GFF files,
are often also compressed when you download them.
These types of files, though, are more commonly decompressed before usage ---
e.g. because they don't take up nearly as much space as a set of FASTQ files.
:::

### `less` to page through files

The previous commands printed file contents to the screen and then returned
your shell prompt.
The `less` command is different, as it **opens** the file in a way that allows
you to browse through it nicely.
And it will display gzip-compressed files in human-readable form!^[
This works because OSC, like most Linux systems, has a helper program
called `lesspipe` set up --- on some other computers, `less` may show you
the same gibberish that `head` did.]
[🥳]{style="font-size:1.2em"}

``` bash
less S63_R1.fastq.gz
```
```bash-out
@ERR10802863.8435456 8435456 length=74
CAACGAATACATCATGTTTGCGAAACTACTCCTCCTCGCCTTGGTGGGGATCAGTACTGCGTACCAGTATGAGT
+
AAAAAEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE
@ERR10802863.27637245 27637245 length=74
GCCACACTTTTGAAGAACAGCGTCATTGTTCTTAATTTTGTCGGCAACGCCTGCACGAGCCTTCCACGTAAGTT
+
AAAAAEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEAEE<EEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE
@ERR10802863.10009244 10009244 length=73
CTCGGCGTTAACTTCATCACGCAGATCATTCCGTTCCAGCAGCTGAAGCAAGACTACCGTCAGTACGAGATGA
+
AAAAAEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEEE
```

When you're inside the `less` pager,
you can **move around** in the file in several ways --- for example:

- By **scrolling** with your mouse.
- With up <kbd>↑</kbd> and down <kbd>↓</kbd> arrows: move **line-by-line**.
- With <kbd>Space</kbd> (down) and <kbd>b</kbd> (back up): move a **full page** at a time.
- By pressing <kbd>G</kbd> to go to the **end** of the file,
  and <kbd>g</kbd> to go (back) to the **top**.

To **exit/quit** `less` and get your shell prompt back, press <kbd>q</kbd>.
(When you do that, no output from the file will remain on the screen.)

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 1: `less`

Open the FASTQ file with `less S63_R1.fastq.gz`, then:

a. Move around a bit using the keys listed above.
b. Among the first reads, you should already spot some unusual-looking ones.
   What is unusual about them?
c. Press <kbd>q</kbd> to quit `less` and get your prompt back.

----

d. **Bonus**: Another useful feature of `less` is the ability to search through a file.
  Press <kbd>/</kbd>, type a search pattern, and press <kbd>Enter</kbd>
  to jump to the first match (then <kbd>n</kbd> for the next and <kbd>N</kbd> for the previous match).
  Open the file back up with `less`, then use this feature to find more reads
  like the ones you found in part b. What pattern did you search for?

<details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} Click for the solution.</summary>

A number of reads are much shorter than the others,
and only consist of `N`s, i.e. uncalled bases. For example:

```bash-out-solo
@ERR10802863.11918285 11918285 length=35
NNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNNN
+
###################################
```

To jump to more of these reads, search for a stretch of `N`s:
type `/NNNNN`, press <kbd>Enter</kbd>, and then press <kbd>n</kbd> to go to each next match.
</details>
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
#### The `-S` option to `less` suppresses "line-wrapping" _(Click to expand)_

When lines are too long to fit on your computer screen,
`less` will by default "wrap" them onto the next line on the screen.
That's convenient for reading,
but can be confusing for tabular formats and formats like FASTQ,
because it means that one line on the screen no longer corresponds to one line
in the file.

With the `-S` option to `less`, lines will not be wrapped but will
"run out of the screen" on the right-hand side
(press the right arrow key <kbd>→</kbd> to see that part):

``` bash
less -S S63_R1.fastq.gz
# [output not shown]
```
:::

### `wc -l` to count lines

_(This command doesn't display file contents, but you'll need it in the next section.)_

The **`wc`** command by default counts the number of lines, words, and bytes
in its input ---
but is most commonly used to only **count lines**, with the `-l` option:

```bash
wc -l metadata.tsv
```
```bash-out
23 metadata.tsv
```

This simple operation can be surprisingly useful:
the number of lines **reflects the number of entries** in many file types.
For example, recall that FASTQ files have four lines per read.

## Redirection and the pipe

### Redirection

The regular output that commands print to the screen
(like a list of files by `ls`, or a number of lines by `wc -l`)
is technically called **"standard out"** or in short "*stdout*".
Sometimes, you may want to do something else with this output,
like storing it in a file.
Luckily, this is easy to do with something called "**redirection**".

First, a reminder of what `echo` does without redirection ---
it simply prints the text we provide to the screen:

```bash
echo "plum"
```
```bash-out
plum
```

Now, redirect `echo`'s standard out to a new file `fruits.txt` using
the `>` operator:

```bash
echo "plum" > fruits.txt
```

No output was printed to the screen --- **it went into the file instead**:

```bash
cat fruits.txt
```
```bash-out
plum
```

The **`>`** operator will redirect output to a file with the following rules:

- If the file doesn't exist, it will be *created*.
- If the file does exist, any contents will be *overwritten*.

Redirect another line into that same file:

```bash
echo "fig" > fruits.txt
cat fruits.txt
```
```bash-out
fig
```

That may not have been what we intended!
As explained above, the earlier file content was _overwritten_.
With **`>>`**, however, output is **appended** (added) to a file:

```bash
echo "banana" >> fruits.txt
cat fruits.txt
```
```bash-out
fig
banana
```

::: {.callout-warning collapse="true"}
#### Redirection caveats _(Click to expand)_

- **Never redirect output back to the command's own input file.**
  Because `>` empties an existing file before the command even runs,
  you shouldn't do this even if you want to edit a file in place.
  For example, the command
  `head metadata.tsv > metadata.tsv` would leave you with an empty `metadata.tsv`.
  (More on this in the [self-study section](#dont-redirect-back-to-the-input-file) at the end.)

- **Error messages are not redirected by** `>`.
  Commands print error messages to a separate "stream" called
  standard error (*stderr*). Because `>` only redirects standard out,
  errors are still shown on the screen:

  ```bash
  # [We won't run this in class, but you can try it out yourself.]
  ls fruits.txt nonexistent.txt > ls-out.txt
  ```
  ```bash-out
  ls: cannot access 'nonexistent.txt': No such file or directory
  ```
  ```bash
  cat ls-out.txt
  ```
  ```bash-out
  fruits.txt
  ```

  That is usually a good thing, since you'll notice errors right away.
  You'll run into standard error again later in the course.
:::

### The pipe

Say that you want to count the number of FASTQ files in the `garrigos/fastq` dir.
You could do that as follows:

```bash
# [Hypothetical example, don't run this]
# First, you'd redirect 'ls' output to a file:
ls ../../garrigos/fastq > fastq-files.txt

# Then you'd count the number of lines, i.e. the number of files in that dir:
wc -l fastq-files.txt
```
```bash-out
44 fastq-files.txt
```
```bash
# Finally, you'd remove the file you no longer need:
rm fastq-files.txt
```

_(Wait, doesn't `ls` print several entries per line? Only when printing straight to the screen:
when its output is redirected, `ls` prints one entry per line, so this count is correct.)_

Above, we essentially wrote an "intermediate result" (`fastq-files.txt`) to file,
which we later removed. What if you could avoid having to write this intermediate file?
You can do so with a so-called **pipe**:

```bash
ls ../../garrigos/fastq | wc -l
```
```bash-out
44
```

With the pipe, the output of the command on the left-hand side
(a file listing, in this case) is **redirected into the command on the right-hand side**
(`wc` in this case).
Like many others, the `wc` command will gladly accept input that way
(i.e., via standard in, or *stdin*) instead of via a file name argument.

<details class="details-quiz">
<summary>Compare this output with the earlier `wc -l` output. What's different, and why? *(Click to see the answer)*</summary>

The output no longer includes a file name: `wc` now reads from standard in
rather than from a file, so there is no file name to report.
</details>

To recap, pipes are useful because they avoid having to write/read intermediate
files --- this saves typing, makes the operation quicker, and reduces file clutter.
In the example above,
you don't need to make a `fastq-files.txt` file to count the number of files.
We'll see pipes in action a bunch more in the next section.

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 2: the pipe

a. What do you think the command below does?
   Could you divide the resulting count by 4 to get the total number of reads
   for sample `S63`? Why or why not?

   ```bash
   cat S63_R1.fastq.gz S63_R2.fastq.gz | wc -l
   ```

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} Click for the solution. </summary>

   Like many shell commands, `cat` accepts multiple arguments,
   i.e. it can operate on multiple files.
   In this case, `cat` would simply print the contents of the two files back-to-back
   (con`cat`enate them!).
   Therefore, `wc -l` will count the total number of lines across the two files.

   ```bash
   cat S63_R1.fastq.gz S63_R2.fastq.gz | wc -l
   ```
   ```bash-out
   193612
   ```

   However, you can't get the total number of reads for sample `S63`
   by dividing this count by 4 (recall: one FASTQ read covers 4 lines),
   since the files are compressed:
   compressed and uncompressed line counts for a file are not the same.
   </details>

b. A classmate wants to pipe the output of `ls` into `wc`,
   but accidentally types `>` instead of `|`:

   ```bash
   ls > wc
   ```

   What do you think will happen?
   Then run it, and check what happened, starting with `ls`.

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} Click for the solution. </summary>

   Nothing is printed, and no counting happens.
   Instead, the shell treats the word right after `>` as the name of the output file,
   so it creates a _file_ called `wc` that contains the file listing
   (which even includes `wc` itself!).
   Remove the file with `rm wc`.
   </details>
:::

## Unix data tools

We'll now turn to some commands that may be described as "Unix data tools".
These are especially good for relatively simple data processing and
summarizing steps, and are excellent at dealing with very large files
such as genomics files. We will cover the following commands:

- `grep` to search for text in files
- `cut` to select one or more columns from tabular data
- `sort` to sort lines, or tabular data by column
- `uniq` to remove duplicates

But we'll start by revisiting one of the example data files,
and discussing tabular plain-text files.

### Tabular plain-text files and file extensions

Let's take another look at the first few lines of the now-familiar `metadata.tsv` file:

```bash
head -n 3 metadata.tsv
```
```bash-out
sample_id       time    treatment
S82     10dpi   cathemerium
S75     10dpi   cathemerium
```

"Tabular" files like this one contain data that is arranged in a
rows-and-columns format, i.e. as in a table or an Excel spreadsheet.
Because plain-text files do not have an intrinsic way to define columns,
certain characters are used as **column delimiters** in plain-text tabular files.
Most commonly, these are:

- A **Tab** (<kbd>Tab</kbd>), and such files are often stored with a **`.tsv`** extension for
  Tab-Separated Values ("**TSV** file").
- A **comma** (<kbd>,</kbd>), and such files are often stored with a **`.csv`** extension for
  Comma-Separated Values ("**CSV** file").

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Does a file use Tabs or spaces? You can check with `cat -A`. _(Click to expand)_

From the `head` output above, you can't tell whether the columns are separated
by Tabs or by a bunch of spaces.
The `-A` option of `cat` makes normally invisible characters visible:
Tabs are shown as `^I`, and the end of each line as `$`:

```bash
cat -A metadata.tsv | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
sample_id^Itime^Itreatment$
S82^I10dpi^Icathemerium$
S75^I10dpi^Icathemerium$
```

So, the columns in this file are separated by single Tab characters.

`cat -A` is also useful for spotting Windows-style line endings,
which are common in files created on Windows computers (e.g., exported from Excel).
These show up as `^M$` instead of `$` and can make commands behave unexpectedly.
:::

::: callout-warning
#### Plain-text file extensions are flexible and mostly for human readability

All plain-text files are fundamentally the same, i.e. "just plain-text files".
Therefore, **changing the file extension does not change the file itself.**
Instead, different file extensions are used primarily to make clear
to humans, and to some extent to the computer, what the file contains.

- This applies to all types of plain-text files, like `.txt` and `.tsv`,
  but also genomics files like `.fastq` and script files like `.R`.
- The same is true for compressed files: removing `.gz` from a file name
  (e.g., renaming `annot.gtf.gz` to `annot.gtf`)
  does **not** decompress the file --- it only makes its name misleading.
:::

### `grep` to print lines that match a pattern

The `grep` command is an extremely useful command that searches for specific text
(or text patterns) in a file.
By default, it **prints each line that contains a "match" in full**.

Its basic syntax is `grep "<search-pattern>" <file-path>`.
For example, to print all lines from `metadata.tsv` that contain "relictum":

```bash
grep "relictum" metadata.tsv
```
<pre class="bash-out"><code>S76     10dpi   <span class="match-red">relictum</span>
S80     10dpi   <span class="match-red">relictum</span>
S85     10dpi   <span class="match-red">relictum</span>
S86     10dpi   <span class="match-red">relictum</span>
S71     24hpi   <span class="match-red">relictum</span>
S74     24hpi   <span class="match-red">relictum</span>
S65     24hpi   <span class="match-red">relictum</span>
S68     24hpi   <span class="match-red">relictum</span></code></pre>

Two notes about the above command and output:

1. While not always necessary, it's good practice to **use quotes** (`"..."`)
   around the search pattern like above^[
   Use _double_ quotes by default, like in the examples.
   _Single_ quotes generally work too, but they behave differently in some situations.
   There are some scenarios where omitting the quotes can lead to rather unexpected behavior.].
2. In most terminals, including at OSC, `grep` will highlight the matching part of a line.

Instead of printing matching lines, you can also **count** them with the `-c` option.
For example, how many control samples are in the dataset?

```bash
grep -c "control" metadata.tsv
```
```bash-out
7
```

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Exercise 3: `grep`

a. What output do you expect from the command below?
   Check your answer by executing the command.

   ```bash
   grep -c "contro" metadata.tsv
   ```

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   The command gives the same output as the previous example:
   the shorter pattern `contro` still matches all the `control` lines:

   ```bash
   grep -c "contro" metadata.tsv
   ```
   ```bash-out
   7
   ```
   </details>

b. Based on the output of the above command, how does `grep`'s matching behavior
   seem to differ from globbing with the shell wildcard `*`?

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   While the initial examples also implied this,
   the above example should make it abundantly clear that `grep` does not need
   to match entire lines or words, etc.

   This behavior is very different from globbing with the `*` wildcard,
   where the pattern has to match the entire file name!
   </details>
:::

<hr style="height:1pt; visibility:hidden;" />

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise: more `grep`

a. A classmate wants to count the `24hpi` samples.
   Reasoning that `24hpi` contains a `4` and `10dpi` does not, they run:

   ```bash
   grep -c "4" metadata.tsv
   ```

   Will this give them the correct count? Why or why not?

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   No: it reports `11`, but there are only 10 `24hpi` samples.
   `grep` matches the pattern anywhere in a line, so it also matches the
   `10dpi` sample `S84`. With tabular files, use a pattern specific enough
   to only match the column you have in mind, like `"24hpi"`.
   </details>

b. Count the number of `relictum` samples at the `24hpi` time point
   with a single line of code.

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} Click here for a hint.</summary>
   You can pipe the output of one `grep` command into another `grep` command!
   </details>

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   You can pipe the output of one `grep` command into another:
   the first selects the `24hpi` lines, and the second counts the `relictum` lines among those.

   ```bash
   grep "24hpi" metadata.tsv | grep -c "relictum"
   ```
   ```bash-out
   4
   ```
   </details>
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="false"}
#### Additional useful `grep` options

`grep` has many other useful options, such as:

- `-v` to **invert** the matching, i.e. print all lines that do **not** match the pattern.
- `-i` to **ignore case** (uppercase vs. lowercase) when searching.
- `-n` to print the **line number** for each matching line.
- `-A <n>` and `-B <n>` to print `n` lines **after** and **before** each match.
- `-w` to make a pattern match whole "**words**" only.
- `-r` to search files in directories **recursively**^[
  Note that even without `-r`, `grep` can operate on multiple files:
  you can give multiple file names as arguments or use a wildcard.].
:::

### Operating on compressed files

The `zcat` command is the counterpart of `cat` for gzip-compressed files:
it prints their contents in human-readable form.
By piping `zcat`'s output into `grep` or into any other command,
you can therefore use all the tools you've learned about even with compressed files ---
let's try that with the _Culex pipiens_ genome annotation GTF file:

```bash
# Search for cecropin-related lines in the GTF file:
zcat annot.gtf.gz | grep "cecropin" | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
NC_068937.1     Gnomon  gene    43201550        43201918        .       +       .       gene_id "LOC120426347"; transcript_id ""; db_xref "GeneID:120426347"; description "cecropin-A2-like"; gbkey "Gene"; gene "LOC120426347"; gene_biotype "protein_coding";
NC_068937.1     Gnomon  transcript      43201550        43201918        .       +       .       gene_id "LOC120426347"; transcript_id "XM_039591134.2"; db_xref "GeneID:120426347"; experiment "COORDINATES: polyA evidence [ECO:0006239]"; gbkey "mRNA"; gene "LOC120426347"; model_evidence "Supporting evidence includes similarity to: 26 ESTs, 18 Proteins"; product "cecropin-A2-like"; transcript_biotype "mRNA";
NC_068937.1     Gnomon  exon    43201550        43201708        .       +       .       gene_id "LOC120426347"; transcript_id "XM_039591134.2"; db_xref "GeneID:120426347"; experiment "COORDINATES: polyA evidence [ECO:0006239]"; gene "LOC120426347"; model_evidence "Supporting evidence includes similarity to: 26 ESTs, 18 Proteins"; product "cecropin-A2-like"; transcript_biotype "mRNA"; exon_number "1";
```

_In this week's [exercises](./w4_exercises.qmd) and next week's assignment (GA2),_
_you'll further explore this GTF file._

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
For very large files like this one: if you forget to pipe `zcat` (or `cat`) output
into another command and your screen floods with text,
press <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>C</kbd> to stop it.
:::

### Combining `cut`, `sort`, and `uniq` to create a list

Say you want an **alphabetically sorted list of distinct treatments** in `metadata.tsv`
(that's trivial for this file, because it's small enough to see that information
at a glance --- but the same approach works on a huge GTF file).
To do this, you'll need to learn about three new commands:

- **`cut`** to select, or "cut out", one or more columns from a tabular file.
- **`sort`** to sort/order/arrange rows --- by default alphabetically.
- **`uniq`** to remove duplicates (i.e., keep all distinct/unique entries)
  from a sorted file/list.

We'll build up a small "pipeline" to do this step by step,
piping the output into `head` at every step.
Piping output into `head` is a handy way to quickly check whether
a command works, without printing a large number of lines.

First, we need to get rid of the header line --- otherwise, the column name
`treatment` would end up in our list as if it were one of the treatments.
We can do this with a neat `tail` trick that tells it to **start at** a specific
line using `-n +<starting-line>`:

```bash
# '-n +2' tells tail to start at line 2:
tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | head
```
```bash-out
S82     10dpi   cathemerium
S75     10dpi   cathemerium
S79     10dpi   cathemerium
S83     10dpi   cathemerium
S78     10dpi   control
S84     10dpi   control
S77     10dpi   control
S81     10dpi   control
S76     10dpi   relictum
S80     10dpi   relictum
```

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
Don't forget to make use of the **command history** here!
Press the up arrow key <kbd>↑</kbd> to recall the previous command,
then edit it to create the next command.
:::

Second, select the column of interest with `cut`,
using its **`-f`** ("field") option to specify the desired column(s):

```bash
tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | cut -f 3 | head
```
```bash-out
cathemerium
cathemerium
cathemerium
cathemerium
control
control
control
control
relictum
relictum
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### More `cut` options _(Click to expand)_

To select **multiple columns**, use a comma-separated list, or a range with `-`:

```bash
cut -f 1,3 metadata.tsv | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
sample_id       treatment
S82     cathemerium
S75     cathemerium
```

```bash
cut -f 1-2 metadata.tsv | head -n 3
```
```bash-out
sample_id       time
S82     10dpi
S75     10dpi
```

Note that it is not possible to change the order of columns with `cut`!

The default column **delimiter** that `cut` expects is a Tab.
Therefore, we didn't have to specify the delimiter in the above examples.
But when a file has a different column delimiter,
use the `-d` option --- e.g. `-d ,` for a CSV file:

```bash
# [Don't run this - for illustration only]
# Select the second column in a comma-delimited (CSV) file:
cut -d , -f 2 my-data.csv
```
:::

Third, use `sort` to alphabetically sort the result:

```bash
tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | cut -f 3 | sort | head
```
```bash-out
cathemerium
cathemerium
cathemerium
cathemerium
cathemerium
cathemerium
cathemerium
control
control
control
```

Finally, use `uniq` to keep only distinct values ---
and get rid of `head`, since the command is now complete:

```bash
tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | cut -f 3 | sort | uniq
```
```bash-out
cathemerium
control
relictum
```

#### Generating a frequency table

With a very small modification to this pipeline,
you can generate a "frequency table" instead of a simple list:
a table with the number of times each distinct value occurs.
You only have to add `uniq`'s `-c` option (for **c**ount):

```bash
tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | cut -f 3 | sort | uniq -c
```
```bash-out
      7 cathemerium
      7 control
      8 relictum
```

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Producing a sorted frequency table _(Click to expand)_

These frequency tables can in turn be sorted by most frequent occurrence.

By default, `sort` sorts alphabetically, even when lines start with numbers:
it compares text character by character,
so `10` would come before `9` (because `1` comes before `9`).
To sort numbers by their value instead, use `sort`'s `-n` option.
Here, combine it with `-r` for reverse sorting so the largest numbers go first:

```bash
tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | cut -f 3 | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr
```
```bash-out
      8 relictum
      7 control
      7 cathemerium
```
:::

:::{.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### Sorting based on one or more specific columns _(Click to expand)_
Above, we used `sort` to simply sort a list.
More generally, `sort` will by default perform sorting based on the entire line.
To sort based on one or more columns, the way you've probably done in Excel,
use the `-k` option --- for example:

```bash
# Sort based on the third column:
tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | sort -k3
```

However, `-k3` actually means "sort based on everything from column 3 to the end of the line."
To sort based on a single column only, give both a start and a stop column:

```bash
# Explicitly indicate to sort based on the third column only:
tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | sort -k3,3
```

To sort first by one column and _then_ by another, use `-k` multiple times:

```bash
# Sort first by the third column, then break ties using the second column:
tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | sort -k3,3 -k2,2
```
:::

::: exercise
#### {{< fa user-edit >}} Self-study exercise: `cut`, `sort`, and `uniq`

a. The four pieces below, when combined with pipes (`|`) in the right order,
   produce a frequency table of the **number of samples per time point**.
   In which order should they go?
   Write out the full command and run it ---
   how many `10dpi` and how many `24hpi` samples are there?

   ```bash
   sort
   cut -f 2
   uniq -c
   tail -n +2 metadata.tsv
   ```

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>
   The file comes first, then we select the column, then sort, then count:

   ```bash
   tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | cut -f 2 | sort | uniq -c
   ```
   ```bash-out
        12 10dpi
        10 24hpi
   ```

   So the two time points do _not_ have the same number of samples:
   there are 12 `10dpi` samples and 10 `24hpi` samples.
   </details>

b. What if you forget `sort`?
   Say you run the treatment frequency table pipeline again, but leave out `sort` like so:

   ```bash
   tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | cut -f 3 | uniq -c
   ```

   What do you expect to happen?

   A) The same output as before; `sort` does not affect the counts.
   B) An error message, because `uniq` needs sorted input.
   C) More than three lines, with each treatment appearing several times.
   D) Three lines, but in a different order.

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   The correct answer is **C**.

   `uniq` only compares _adjacent_ lines,
   so without sorting first, it counts each separate "run" of identical values ---
   here, one run per treatment per time point:

   ```bash-out
         4 cathemerium
         4 control
         4 relictum
         3 cathemerium
         3 control
         4 relictum
   ```

   This is why `sort` almost always comes right before `uniq`.
   </details>

c. Using a pipeline similar to those above to create another frequency table,
   check whether any duplicate sample IDs are present in `metadata.tsv`.

   <details><summary> {{< fa check-circle >}} _Click for the solution._ </summary>

   To check for duplicate sample IDs, create a frequency table of the first column
   (sample IDs):

   ```bash
   tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | cut -f 1 | sort | uniq -c
   ```

   This produces one line per sample (22 in total), and every single one shows a
   count of 1. That means there are no duplicate sample IDs:
   if any sample ID were duplicated, its count would be 2 or higher.

   Even better/more elegant: instead of scanning all 22 lines yourself,
   add `sort -nr | head -n 1` to the end of the pipeline. This sorts the counts
   from high to low and shows only the top line.
   If that single count is 1, you immediately know there are no duplicates:

   ```bash
   tail -n +2 metadata.tsv | cut -f 1 | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr | head -n 1
   ```
   ```bash-out
         1 S86
   ```
   </details>

:::

## Self-study: The Unix philosophy and data streaming

In this lecture, and in particular with these Unix data tool examples,
we saw the Unix philosophy in action:

> *This is the Unix philosophy: Write programs that do one thing and do it well.*
> *Write programs to work together.*
> *Write programs to handle text **streams**, because that is a universal interface.*
> <br> --- Doug McIlroy

Some advantages of a modular approach are that it's easier to spot errors,
to swap out components, and to learn.

### Text/data streaming

What about those **text "streams"** mentioned in the quote above?
Rather than loading entire files into memory,
most Unix tools process them one line at a time
(a notable exception is `sort`, which has to see all lines before it can output anything).
This is very useful when working with large files in particular! For example,
`head` **prints results instantly even for a 10 TB file** that could never be loaded
into memory.
By contrast, try to take a peek at such a file with a GUI text editor,
and it will freeze or refuse to open the file.

Here is one other example,
combining the `cat` command with globbing and redirection.
This command would concatenate (combine) all your R1 FASTQ files into a single file.
This code is elegantly short,
and will run quickly without using much computer memory!

```bash
# [Don't run this - for illustration only]
cat ../../garrigos/fastq/*R1.fastq.gz > all_R1.fastq.gz
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false"}
#### How does the above command work?

1. `cat` is presented with a list of all R1 FASTQ files in the `garrigos/fastq` dir:
   the shell expands the glob pattern `*R1.fastq.gz` into a list of matching files,
   and passes that list to `cat` as arguments.

2. `cat` then reads each file in turn, and prints its contents:
   When it prints multiple files, it simply prints them one after the other,
   i.e. concatenates them.

3. The concatenated output is redirected to the file `all_R1.fastq.gz`.
   That is in fact a valid compressed FASTQ file, because:
   - FASTQ files can be concatenated freely since every read is a
   "stand-alone" unit of 4 lines.
   - Gzipped (`.gz`) files can also be concatenated freely!
:::

### Don't redirect back to the input file!

One thing you should never do is redirect the output of a command
"back" to its own input file.
This doesn't just fail --- it **destroys the input file**,
because the shell empties the file to prepare it for the output
_before_ the command has had a chance to read it.

```bash
# [Don't run this - for illustration only]
# You should NEVER run something like this:
sort metadata.tsv > metadata.tsv
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
#### How to change the original file _(Click to expand)_

Therefore, if you really want to edit the original file instead of creating a
separate edited copy, you will need two steps:

1. Redirect to a new, edited copy of the input file.
2. Rename the copy to overwrite the original file.

```bash
# [Don't run this - for illustration only]
# Step 1 - redirect to a new file:
sort metadata.tsv > metadata_sorted.tsv

# Step 2 - rename the new file to overwrite the original (if really needed!)
mv metadata_sorted.tsv metadata.tsv
```

However, I generally recommend that whenever you edit files,
you keep both the original and the edited version ---
so you won't typically need the above roundabout method.
:::
